title: Investigation process (Authorised Professional Practice: Investigation)
edition_version: APP page first published 23 Oct 2013; updated 8 Oct 2026
key_findings: Investigative mindset: investigators should be professionally curious, impartial yet empathetic, and pursue reasonable lines of enquiry that point both towards and away from a suspect.
Current wording of the ABC principle on the page (updated 8 Oct 2026): 'Assume nothing, Believe nothing, Challenge everything', framed as a way to secure best evidence.

Defines a hypothesis as "a supposition or proposed explanation based on limited evidence"; advises developing alternative hypotheses from the same material to generate lines of enquiry and testing them as material arrives (worked example discounts several).

Investigators must record decisions and the supporting rationale (e.g., a no-further-action decision) in auditable records; decision logs are listed among early-stage logs; review can be self, peer, expert or formal.
athar_applications: Canonical anchor for ATHAR's reasoning loop: 'generate alternatives' and 'log decisions with reasons' steps.
Case-design fairness rule: every case must contain meaningful lines of enquiry that point away from the most obvious suspect.
Teen-friendly re-voicing of ABC as 'verify, don't assume' rather than 'distrust everyone'.
limitations: Professional practice guidance for England and Wales, not empirical evidence; the ABC slogan itself has no validation study.
'Believe nothing' can be misread as cynicism towards victims and witnesses; APP pairs it with empathy.
The term 'policy file' does not appear on this page (decision logs and an investigation management document do).
Non-commercial licence: ATHAR may cite and paraphrase concepts but must not reproduce text commercially without a College licence.

title: Investigative interviewing (Authorised Professional Practice)
edition_version: APP online version consulted 2026-10-27; first-published date not shown on page
key_findings: PEACE has five phases: Planning and preparation; Engage and explain; Account, clarify and challenge; Closure; Evaluation.

Seven interviewing principles include accuracy and reliability, fairness (extra care with vulnerable people), an investigative mindset that tests accounts against known facts, wide but not unfair or oppressive questioning, and persistence that is not unfair in itself.
Challenging inconsistencies is part of the Account phase but is done without raising the voice; evaluation covers both the account and the interviewer's own performance.
Refers to free recall and to the Ministry of Justice 'Achieving Best Evidence' (2022) guidance as largely compatible with PEACE.
athar_applications: Template for ATHAR's in-game interview scenes: plan -> engage -> account -> clarify -> close -> evaluate.
Evaluation phase maps to an after-interview reflection prompt that scores the player's question quality, not the suspect's 'breaking'.
limitations: Practice guidance; PEACE's superiority rests on research summarised elsewhere (e.g., ATH-SRC-0420), with few field RCTs.
Designed for UK adversarial context; Arab criminal procedure (prosecutor-led, inquisitorial elements) differs.

title: Intelligence report (Authorised Professional Practice: Intelligence management) - 3x5x2 grading
key_findings: UK police use a 3x5x2 system: source evaluation (reliable / untested / not reliable), information assessment (A-E) and handling codes (P / C).

Information grades turn on how the source knows: A known directly (e.g., witnessed); B known indirectly but corroborated by independent information; C known indirectly only; D cannot be assessed (e.g., anonymous); E suspected false, with reasons documented.
An 'untested' source's information should be treated with caution and corroboration considered before action; the older 5x5x5 system is referenced only for historic intelligence.
athar_applications: Directly adaptable two-axis grading for in-game sources: 'Who is the source?' x 'How do they know?'.
Teaches that corroboration only counts when it is independent (grade B requires independent information).
limitations: Built for handling intelligence, not for weighing courtroom evidence; grades are human judgments and the page reports no inter-rater reliability data.
ATHAR should adapt concepts in its own wording; the text is under a non-commercial licence.

title: Principles on Effective Interviewing for Investigations and Information Gathering (Mendez Principles)
publisher: Association for the Prevention of Torture (APT) and partners
edition_version: Adopted May 2021; available in Arabic and ~23 other languages
key_findings: Six principles: foundations in science, law and ethics; practice as a comprehensive process with legal safeguards; identifying and addressing vulnerability; specific training; accountability (including audio-visual recording); national implementation (including judicial exclusion of coerced statements).
Aims to move practice from coercive interrogation to rapport-based interviewing that yields accurate and reliable information.
Describes coercive methods as ineffective and counterproductive, raising risks of unreliable information and miscarriages of justice.
An official Arabic version exists (APT lists Arabic among available languages).
athar_applications: Normative backbone for ETHICAL_INVESTIGATION_PRINCIPLES: ATHAR interview mechanics must be rapport-based and never reward coercion.
Arabic version allows faithful Arabic terminology for teaching ethical questioning.
limitations: Non-binding soft-law instrument; its effectiveness claims rest on a research base with relatively few field experiments (see ATH-SRC-0420, ATH-SRC-0422).
No reuse licence stated (page marked (c) APT); cite and paraphrase only.

title: UN Manual on Investigative Interviewing for Criminal Investigation
authors: United Nations Department of Peace Operations
Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights
United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime
key_findings: Described by the drafting secretariat (Norwegian Centre for Human Rights, with Ivar Fahsing) as the first 'One UN' manual on criminal investigation, produced jointly by DPO, OHCHR and UNODC (2024).
athar_applications: Candidate reference for expert reviewers when checking that ATHAR interview scenes match the international standard.
limitations: Full manual PDF read on 2026-10-27 (gap-fill); its content is summarised in ATH-SRC-0453 (same publication). Reuse terms not stated.

title: The Cognitive Interview: A meta-analytic review and study space analysis of the past 25 years
key_findings: Study-space analysis of 57 articles (65 experiments) and meta-analysis of 46 articles on the Cognitive Interview (CI).
Replicates a large increase in correct details with a small increase in errors; confabulation rates did not differ between CI and control interviews.
Effects held when modified CI versions were included; older adult witnesses appeared to benefit more; field tests suggested trained officers obtained more information.
athar_applications: Justifies an ATHAR witness mechanic where open, context-reinstating questions unlock more correct details, while still carrying a small error rate the player must check.
limitations: Mostly laboratory studies with mock events; the small rise in incorrect details means more recall is not automatically better evidence.
Abstract read via OpenAlex index; exact effect sizes not extracted.

title: The Cognitive Interview method of conducting police interviews: Eliciting extensive information and promoting Therapeutic Jurisprudence
edition_version: International Journal of Law and Psychiatry 33(5-6):321-328
key_findings: Fisher & Geiselman argue police receive little training for interviewing cooperative witnesses and so elicit less information than is available; they analyse which typical-interview components limit recall and describe the Cognitive Interview as an alternative that enhances recollection and likely supports victims' well-being (PubMed abstract).
athar_applications: Authoritative originator reference for the CI components ATHAR may simulate (to be confirmed against full text).
limitations: Abstract read via PubMed (2026-10-27 gap-fill); the list of CI components must still be taken from the full text before being enumerated as fact.

title: Identifying the Culprit: Assessing Eyewitness Identification
authors: Committee on Scientific Approaches to Understanding and Maximizing the Validity and Reliability of Eyewitness Identification in Law Enforcement and the Courts
key_findings: Recommends double-blind lineup/photo-array administration, standardized witness instructions stating the perpetrator may not be present, and video recording of identification procedures.
Recommends documenting the witness's confidence verbatim at the first identification and avoiding feedback that could shift confidence.

Recommends training for officers (including dispatchers not passing information between callers), pretrial judicial inquiry, and scientific-framework expert testimony that does not opine on a specific identification.
Calls for more research on interacting system and estimator variables (e.g., weapon presence, stress) and caution before changing procedures until evidence is clear.
athar_applications: ATHAR witness logs must store the first confidence statement; later 'certainty' in a witness is flagged as possibly contaminated.
Design rule: no in-game lineup without a 'the person may not be here' instruction; teaches system-variable thinking.
limitations: US-focused legal recommendations; committee was cautious about some procedures (e.g., sequential vs simultaneous lineups) pending more research.

title: The Relationship Between Eyewitness Confidence and Identification Accuracy: A New Synthesis
edition_version: Psychological Science in the Public Interest 18(1):10-65
key_findings: Under 'pristine' conditions, initial confidence and accuracy are strongly related for adults and high-confidence suspect identifications are highly accurate.
Pristine conditions: an initial, uncontaminated test; a fair lineup; no administrator influence; an immediate confidence statement.
Under non-pristine conditions (e.g., unfair lineups) even high-confidence identifications can be seriously unreliable; confidence expressed later (e.g., at trial) is not the diagnostic signal.
athar_applications: Corrects the folk belief 'confident witness = reliable' and the opposite overcorrection 'eyewitnesses are worthless'; ATHAR teaches 'first, uncontaminated confidence matters'.
Character pattern: a witness whose confidence grows across scenes after feedback (see KO-CD-05-001).
limitations: Conclusions apply to initial tests under specified conditions; many jurisdictions have not adopted the reforms that create them.
Debated in the field (e.g., how to weigh low-confidence IDs); full text accessed only via abstract.

title: Policy and procedure recommendations for the collection and preservation of eyewitness identification evidence
key_findings: AP-LS scientific review paper proposing nine recommendations; four carried over from 1998 (filler selection, pre-lineup instructions, double-blind administration, recording confidence).

Five new recommendations: interview the witness before the lineup, require evidence-based suspicion before any identification procedure, video-record the whole procedure, avoid repeated identifications of the same suspect by the same witness, and avoid or improve showups.
Reliability of eyewitness evidence depends heavily on how it is collected and preserved.
athar_applications: 'Evidence-based suspicion before an identification' becomes a gameplay gate: players must justify why a character is in a lineup.
limitations: Consensus recommendations by six senior researchers; some items remain contested and are US-procedure specific.

title: Planting misinformation in the human mind: A 30-year investigation of the malleability of memory
key_findings: Review of ~30 years of research: exposure to misleading post-event information can impair memory of the original event (misinformation effect).
Warnings about misinformation reduce its effect only in limited circumstances; some groups are more susceptible than others.
Research extends to rich false memories of whole events that never happened.
athar_applications: Mechanic: a leading question or a gossiping character can permanently alter a witness's later account; the game tracks contamination sources.
limitations: Author's own synthesis; the false-memory strand (e.g., implanted childhood events) has been debated over effect prevalence and generalisability to real cases.

title: Reconstruction of automobile destruction: An example of the interaction between language and memory
edition_version: Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior 13(5):585-589
key_findings: Classic study on how the wording of a question about a filmed car accident relates to witnesses' later reports (bibliographic record verified; abstract withheld).
athar_applications: Historical anchor for teaching that the verb chosen in a question can shape an answer; use only as illustration, not as sole evidence.
limitations: Small student samples, lab film stimuli; findings not re-read in this session; cite via the later review ATH-SRC-0410.

title: Suggestibility of the child witness: A historical review and synthesis
key_findings: Concludes there are reliable age differences in suggestibility, with younger children generally more suggestible.
Even very young children can recall much forensically relevant information - youth does not make testimony useless.
Proposes cognitive, social and biological factor families to explain apparently contradictory findings.
athar_applications: Grounds a younger-witness character whose account is accurate on core details but vulnerable to suggestive questioning; teaches care, not dismissal.
limitations: 1993 synthesis; later research refines age effects and interviewing protocols; abstract read via OpenAlex index.

title: Accuracy of Deception Judgments
publisher: SAGE / Society for Personality and Social Psychology
key_findings: Meta-analysis of 206 documents and 24,483 judges: average lie-truth accuracy about 54%, where chance is 50%.
Truths were classified correctly more often (~61%) than lies (~47%), reflecting a truth bias.
Experts did not outperform non-experts; lies were detected less well from video-only cues than from audio or transcripts.
athar_applications: Hard design rule: ATHAR never lets body language, nervousness or eye contact count as evidence of lying.
Myth-busting micro-lesson: 'even professionals are near chance at spotting lies from behaviour'.
limitations: Mostly low-stakes laboratory lies told by students; high-stakes real-world lies may differ (but field evidence has not shown reliable cues).
Accessed via a reproduction of the published article (ACLU FOIA archive); DOI taken from the article.

title: Why do lie-catchers fail? A lens model meta-analysis of human lie judgments
key_findings: Lens-model meta-analyses show the weak link in lie detection is the scarcity of valid behavioural cues, not mainly that judges use the wrong cues.
Judges' perceived cues correlated substantially with actual cues; eye contact was only weakly related to deception judgments despite popular belief.
Improvement may depend on methods that increase behavioural differences between liars and truth-tellers rather than on teaching cue lists.
athar_applications: Supports teaching 'check statements against evidence' instead of 'read the face'; informs evidence-disclosure mechanics.
limitations: Meta-analytic estimates depend on lab paradigms; accessed via reproduction (ACLU FOIA archive).

title: Reading Lies: Nonverbal Communication and Deception
key_findings: Concludes that nonverbal cues to deceit found so far are "faint and unreliable".
People perform only moderately at lie detection when they focus on behaviour, and misbeliefs about nonverbal deception cues are hard to correct.
athar_applications: Explicit citation for the brief's rule that body-language lie detection is presented as unreliable; content for a 'myth vs science' card.
limitations: Review by researchers who also develop verbal lie-detection approaches; abstract-level access only.

title: "I'm innocent!": Effects of training on judgments of truth and deception in the interrogation room
key_findings: Observers watching mock-crime interrogations generally could not distinguish truthful from deceptive suspects.
Observers trained in verbal and nonverbal deception cues were less accurate than untrained observers, yet more confident and gave more reasons for their judgments.
athar_applications: Key evidence for a 'confidence is not accuracy' lesson; ATHAR must not sell a 'lie-spotting' skill tree.
limitations: Small samples (16 suspects, 40 observers) and mock crimes; training content was a specific commercial-style method.

title: The Polygraph and Lie Detection
key_findings: Consensus study reviewing evidence on polygraph use in criminal investigation, employment screening and counter-intelligence, including countermeasures and alternatives (voice-stress, brain measures).

Executive summary concludes that, for examinees untrained in countermeasures, specific-incident polygraph tests discriminate lying from truth at rates well above chance but well below perfection; generalising to screening is not justified and screening accuracy is almost certainly lower.
Its worked example shows that in a population with very few deceivers, a threshold catching most of them would flag about 1,600 innocent people per 10,000 tested.
athar_applications: Background for a myth card: machines that 'detect lies' measure arousal, not deception; ATHAR should not include a polygraph-as-truth gadget.
limitations: Executive summary read 2026-10-27 (gap-fill); 2003 evidence base; research quality described by the committee as far short of desirable.

title: Police-induced confessions: Risk factors and recommendations
key_findings: Official AP-LS white paper reviewing suspect characteristics (dispositional risk, e.g., youth) and interrogation tactics (situational risk) that increase false confessions.
Central recommendation: mandatory electronic recording of entire interrogations; further reforms proposed for consideration.
athar_applications: Grounds the CD pattern of a young character who confesses falsely; ATHAR treats any confession as a claim needing independent corroboration.
limitations: Built mainly on US wrongful-conviction cases and lab paradigms; updated by ATH-SRC-0419.

title: Police-induced confessions, 2.0: Risk factors and recommendations
key_findings: Updates the 2010 paper to cover consequences of false confessions (e.g., contaminating other evidence, guilty pleas, juries) and science-based alternatives to accusatorial interviewing.

Seven reforms, including full recording, evidence-based suspicion before guilt-presumptive questioning, time limits, banning false-evidence ploys and leniency-implying minimization, and attorneys/appropriate adults for youthful suspects.
Reports that adolescents are especially susceptible to false-evidence tactics and short-term escape motives; cites a survey in which 17% of youthful detainees said they had falsely confessed.
athar_applications: Defines what ATHAR must never reward: deception about evidence, implied leniency, exhausting or isolating a character.
Supports keeping confessions from contaminating other in-game evidence (shield forensic results from confession knowledge).
limitations: Self-report figures (e.g., 17%) are not prevalence estimates; US-centred legal framing; read via full-text copy hosted by an advocacy site and APA summary.

title: Accusatorial and information-gathering interrogation methods and their effects on true and false confessions: a meta-analytic review
key_findings: Meta-analysis of 5 field studies and 12 experiments comparing accusatorial and information-gathering methods.

In experiments, information-gathering preserved or increased true confessions while reducing false confessions; accusatorial methods increased both true and false confessions relative to direct questioning.
Authors caution that the small number of independent samples limits confidence.
athar_applications: Evidence that ATHAR's rapport/information-gathering interview design is not just 'nicer' but yields better-quality information.
limitations: Few independent samples; field studies could not isolate diagnosticity.

title: Taking responsibility for an act not committed: The influence of age and suggestibility
key_findings: Lab experiment with 12-13-year-olds, 15-16-year-olds and young adults falsely accused of crashing a computer; half were shown false evidence of liability.
Younger participants were more suggestible and more likely than older participants to falsely take responsibility.
athar_applications: Developmental grounding for portraying teen characters as more vulnerable to pressure; never as a technique for players.
limitations: Low-stakes lab analogue (computer-crash paradigm); exact rates not extracted; abstract read via OpenAlex index.

title: Why tough tactics fail and rapport gets results: Observing Rapport-Based Interpersonal Techniques (ORBIT) to generate useful information from terrorists
key_findings: Field coding of 418 video-recorded police interviews (~288 hours; 58 interviewers) with suspects later convicted of terrorism-related offences.

Rapport-based, motivational-interviewing-style interviewer behaviour was associated with more adaptive suspect behaviour and higher information yield; even minimal maladaptive behaviour reduced yield.
athar_applications: Supports scoring players on rapport and open questioning; characters 'open up' in response to respect, not intimidation.
limitations: Correlational field data from one national context; coded behaviours are not randomly assigned.

title: Strategic use of evidence during police interviews: When training to detect deception works
key_findings: Police trainees (N=82) were trained or not trained to use evidence strategically (withholding it and probing) when interviewing lying or truthful mock suspects.
Liars interviewed by trained interviewers were more inconsistent with the evidence; trained interviewers relied on a statement-evidence consistency cue.
Deception-detection accuracy: 85.4% for trained vs 56.1% for untrained interviewers.
athar_applications: Mechanic: players choose when to reveal a clue; inconsistency between a statement and known evidence (not demeanour) is the signal - safe, non-coercive alternative to 'reading' suspects.
limitations: Single lab mock-crime study with trainees; real suspects may adapt counter-strategies; abstract-level access via OpenAlex. Must be taught as reasoning about evidence, not as an interrogation tactic.

title: The Multiple Dimensions of Tunnel Vision in Criminal Cases
publisher: University of Wisconsin Law School (Wisconsin Law Review)
key_findings: Analyses tunnel vision as a product of cognitive biases, institutional pressures and procedural rules that lead investigators and prosecutors to focus on a suspect and filter out contrary evidence (citation confirmed via author's official CV; content summary corroborated by secondary description).
athar_applications: Primary framing for ATHAR's 'tunnel vision' error and its detection signal (single-hypothesis fixation).
limitations: Law-review analysis built on case studies of US exonerations rather than controlled experiments; full text not read this session.

title: Prime suspect: An examination of factors that aggravate and counteract confirmation bias in criminal investigations
key_findings: Experimental examination of factors that aggravate and counteract confirmation bias in criminal investigations (record verified; abstract withheld by publisher in all catalogs checked).
athar_applications: If findings are confirmed (expert check), justifies delaying a formal 'name your suspect' moment and prompting players to argue the suspect's innocence.
limitations: Abstract not accessible this session; specific findings must be verified before being cited.

title: Let's find the evidence: an analogue study of confirmation bias in criminal investigations
edition_version: Journal of Investigative Psychology and Offender Profiling 7(3):231-246
key_findings: Three studies: participants read a case file and chose additional investigations (incriminating or exonerating); choices followed their initial view of the suspect's guilt.
Selecting incriminating investigations increased with crime severity and evidence strength, and was associated with conviction rates.
Nuance: incriminating choices rarely exceeded 50% of selections, so bias was present but not overwhelming.
athar_applications: Ready-made task pattern: 'choose your next three enquiries' with incriminating vs exonerating options, logged as a bias indicator.
limitations: Student/lay analogue samples; effect modest; not professional investigators.

title: The forensic confirmation bias: Problems, perspectives, and proposed solutions
publisher: Elsevier / Society for Applied Research in Memory and Cognition
edition_version: Journal of Applied Research in Memory and Cognition 2(1):42-52
key_findings: Uses the Mayfield fingerprint misidentification and the NAS 2009 critique to argue forensic judgments are vulnerable to contextual bias.

Reviews evidence that contextual information such as a confession can bias lay witnesses' perceptions and memories and experts' judgments across forensic disciplines; proposes best practices to limit bias.
athar_applications: Mechanic: if the player shares a confession with the lab character, later 'results' are flagged as context-exposed; teaches evidence independence.
limitations: Review/position paper; specific debiasing procedures not verified from abstract.

title: The making of an expert detective: the role of experience in English and Norwegian police officers' investigative decision-making
key_findings: 124 officers reviewed two semi-fictitious cases and listed hypotheses and actions, scored against a gold standard set by senior homicide experts.
Experienced English detectives produced far more gold-standard hypotheses and actions than novices; in Norway experience made no difference.
Authors attribute the difference to England's structured investigator accreditation (PIP), suggesting experience alone does not build expertise.
athar_applications: Validated assessment design: count and quality of relevant hypotheses/actions against an expert-built gold standard (basis for KO-LA-05-001).
Supports deliberate, structured practice rather than just 'playing more cases'.
limitations: Quasi-experimental; country and training differences confounded; adult professionals, not teens.

title: Psychology of Intelligence Analysis
publisher: Center for the Study of Intelligence, Central Intelligence Agency
key_findings: Collects articles written 1978-1986; chapters cover perception, memory, keeping an open mind, structuring problems, Analysis of Competing Hypotheses (Ch. 8, pp. 95-110) and biases in evaluating evidence, cause-effect, probability and hindsight.
Describes 'satisficing' - choosing the first hypothesis that seems good enough - as a common weak strategy for choosing among hypotheses.

ACH (Ch. 8) is an eight-step procedure: list all reasonable hypotheses (ideally with a diverse group); list evidence and arguments; build a hypotheses-by-evidence matrix and judge diagnosticity; drop non-diagnostic items; try to disprove rather than prove; test sensitivity to a few critical items; report the relative likelihood of all hypotheses; set milestones that would signal change.
The most probable hypothesis is usually the one with the least evidence against it, not the most evidence for it.
Ch. 10 reports that impressions tend to persist even after the evidence that created them is fully discredited.
athar_applications: Conceptual source for ATHAR's 'hypothesis board' and 'diagnosticity' teaching; chapter titles map to the reasoning-error catalog.
limitations: Classic but largely theory- and experience-based; controlled tests of ACH show mixed results (ATH-SRC-0430).
Chapter 8 read from the full CIA PDF on 2026-10-27 (gap-fill): eight-step ACH procedure confirmed; Chapter 10 section 'Persistence of Impressions Based on Discredited Evidence' also confirmed.
US-government publication; public-domain status of all parts not confirmed.

title: The "analysis of competing hypotheses" in intelligence analysis
key_findings: Randomised experiment with 50 intelligence analysts on a hypothesis-testing task with probabilistic ground truth.
ACH-trained analysts did not follow all ACH steps; evidence that ACH reduced confirmation bias was mixed, and ACH may have increased judgment inconsistency and error.
athar_applications: Warning against shipping a heavy ACH matrix to teens as the 'scientific method'; use a light 'evidence vs hypotheses' board and test learning effects.
limitations: Single study, modest sample of professionals; task differs from narrative mystery reasoning.

title: A Tradecraft Primer: Structured Analytic Techniques for Improving Intelligence Analysis
publisher: Central Intelligence Agency (Center for the Study of Intelligence)
key_findings: ACH weighs each item of evidence against all hypotheses, rating consistency; the aim is to disprove rather than confirm, and hypotheses with fewest inconsistencies are strongest; asks what evidence should exist but is missing.
Key Assumptions Check: state the analytic line, list premises, challenge each, keep only those that must hold (illustrated with the 2002 Washington sniper case narrowing on wrong assumptions).
Also describes Devil's Advocacy, Indicators/Signposts and Quality of Information Check; states techniques do not guarantee accuracy but improve rigour and transparency.
athar_applications: Source of teen-adaptable tools: 'What must be true?' (assumptions), 'What's missing?' (absent evidence), 'Argue the other side' (devil's advocate).
limitations: Practitioner guide without empirical validation of each technique; US public-domain status assumed for a US-government work (commercial reuse to be confirmed by legal team).

title: Intelligence Community Directive 203: Analytic Standards
authors: Office of the Director of National Intelligence
publisher: Office of the Director of National Intelligence (US)
key_findings: Nine tradecraft standards include describing source quality and credibility, expressing uncertainty, distinguishing information from assumptions/judgments, analysing alternatives, and explaining changes in judgments.

Seven likelihood bands with fixed terms: almost no chance/remote (01-05%), very unlikely (05-20%), unlikely (20-45%), roughly even chance (45-55%), likely (55-80%), very likely (80-95%), almost certain (95-99%).
Confidence in an assessment is distinct from likelihood of the event, and the two must not be combined in the same sentence.
athar_applications: Basis for ATHAR's uncertainty ladder and for separating 'how likely?' from 'how solid is my evidence?' in player conclusions.
limitations: Designed for professional intelligence products; seven bands may be too fine for 13-15-year-olds; Arabic equivalents need testing for consistent interpretation.

title: Words of Estimative Probability
publisher: Central Intelligence Agency, Studies in Intelligence
edition_version: Studies in Intelligence vol. 8 no. 4 (per CIA archive URL path); declassified 1993
key_findings: Shows that vague probability phrases are read very differently: one estimate's 'serious possibility' was interpreted by readers as anywhere from about 20% to 80%.
Proposes a small fixed vocabulary tied to numeric ranges (e.g., 'probable' ~75%, 'chances about even' ~50%) and reserving 'possible' for when likelihood cannot be estimated.
athar_applications: Classroom-ready story for why ATHAR shows numbers next to Arabic probability words.
limitations: Year inferred from internal text and archive path; anecdotal evidence base; superseded in practice by ICD 203 scales.

title: Communicating uncertainty using words and numbers
key_findings: Communicators prefer verbal probability terms even in high-stakes domains, and such terms can serve aims other than conveying uncertainty (e.g., protecting credibility).
Verbal terms are easily misunderstood, and attaching imprecise numeric ranges to them does not reliably prevent miscommunication.
Recipients making consequential decisions prefer precise numeric probabilities.
athar_applications: Challenges a words-only ladder: ATHAR should show numbers alongside Arabic terms and test comprehension rather than assume ICD-style ranges solve ambiguity.
limitations: Review article; abstract-level access via OpenAlex index; evidence base largely Western, English-language.

title: Universal Declaration of Human Rights
key_findings: Art. 11(1): a person charged with a penal offence is presumed innocent until proved guilty according to law in a public trial with defence guarantees.
Art. 12: protection against arbitrary interference with privacy, family, home or correspondence and attacks on honour and reputation.
athar_applications: Foundational text for ATHAR's 'suspect is not guilty' language rules and its anti-doxxing/privacy rules.
limitations: Declaration (not a treaty); legal effect varies; ATHAR uses it for values, not legal advice.

title: International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights
title_ar: العهد الدولي الخاص بالحقوق المدنية والسياسية
edition_version: GA resolution 2200A (XXI), adopted 16 Dec 1966; in force 23 Mar 1976
key_findings: Art. 14(2): everyone charged with a criminal offence is presumed innocent until proved guilty according to law.
Art. 14(3)(g): no one may be compelled to testify against themselves or to confess guilt.
Art. 7 prohibits torture and cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment; Art. 17 protects privacy, family, home, correspondence, honour and reputation.
athar_applications: Legal grounding for the rule that in-game confessions obtained by pressure are worthless and that suspects keep rights in fiction too.
limitations: Binding on States parties, not on private actors; ATHAR uses it as a normative reference.

title: Convention on the Rights of the Child
edition_version: GA resolution 44/25, adopted 20 Nov 1989; in force 2 Sep 1990
key_findings: Art. 16: children are protected from arbitrary or unlawful interference with privacy and attacks on honour and reputation.
Art. 40(2)(b): a child accused of infringing penal law is presumed innocent, may not be compelled to give testimony or confess guilt, and has privacy respected at all stages of proceedings.
athar_applications: Directly relevant to ATHAR's 13-17 users and teen characters: no naming/shaming of minor suspects; privacy-first storytelling.
limitations: State obligations; use as values framework, coordinate with Library 11 (rights & safety).

title: Arab Charter on Human Rights
edition_version: Adopted 22 May 2004; entered into force 15 Mar 2008 (English translation consulted)
key_findings: Art. 16: the accused is presumed innocent until proved guilty by a final judgment, with minimum guarantees, including the right not to be compelled to testify against oneself or confess guilt (16(6)).
Art. 8 prohibits torture and cruel, degrading or inhuman treatment; Art. 21 protects privacy, family, home, correspondence, honour and reputation.
athar_applications: Lets ATHAR ground its ethics in a regional Arab instrument, not only UN/Western sources - important for credibility with Arab educators and parents.
limitations: Verified via University of Minnesota Human Rights Library English translation; the official Arabic text from the League of Arab States must be used for Arabic wording; ratification varies by state; criticised by human-rights bodies on some provisions (not reviewed here).

title: Berkeley Protocol on Digital Open Source Investigations: A Practical Guide on the Effective Use of Digital Open Source Information in Investigating Violations of International Criminal, Human Rights and Humanitarian Law
authors: Human Rights Center, UC Berkeley School of Law
key_findings: Professional principles (accountability, competency, objectivity incl. testing multiple working hypotheses, legality, security awareness), methodological principles (accuracy, data minimization, preservation, security by design) and ethical principles (dignity, humility, inclusivity, independence, transparency).
Investigation cycle: online inquiries, preliminary assessment, collection, preservation, verification, investigative analysis.
Public information can still raise privacy concerns; the 'mosaic effect' can re-identify people by combining datasets; safety includes digital, physical and psychosocial wellbeing.
athar_applications: Ethics frame for any ATHAR digital-clue mechanic: fictional data only, data minimization, no real-person searching.
Arabic edition supports accurate Arabic terminology.
limitations: Written for professional international-justice investigations, not for teen learners; must be simplified and never encourage real-world OSINT on real people.

title: Verification Handbook (A definitive guide to verifying digital content for emergency coverage; and later editions on disinformation and investigative reporting)
edition_version: Original edition (site footer (c) 2013-2016); later 'For Disinformation and Media Manipulation' edition; Arabic translation of original edition
key_findings: Practitioner handbook series offering step-by-step guidance for verifying user-generated content, images and video; available in Arabic among other translations.
athar_applications: Reference for designing fictional 'verify the photo/post' puzzles (source, date, location checks) with fictional data.
limitations: Journalism practice, not peer-reviewed; edition years and licence not stated on the pages consulted; tools named may be outdated.

title: Criminal Procedure and Investigations Act 1996, section 23 (Code of practice)
edition_version: As amended (s.23(6) substituted 2018); Code of Practice issued under s.23(1), current version published 23 Nov 2020
key_findings: Requires a code of practice ensuring that in a criminal investigation all reasonable steps are taken and, in particular, all reasonable lines of inquiry are pursued.
Requires relevant material to be recorded, retained and revealed to the prosecution, and then disclosed to the accused where required.
athar_applications: Legal grounding for ATHAR's fairness rule: an investigation must follow lines that could clear a suspect, and keep a record others can check.
limitations: England and Wales only; the Code's paragraph wording ('towards or away from the suspect') was not fetched this session - that phrasing is confirmed in APP (ATH-SRC-0400).

title: Research Resources (Innocence Project)
edition_version: Web page consulted 2026-10-27; data 'as of January 2020'
key_findings: Reports that roughly 25% of the 375+ DNA exonerees it documented (as of January 2020) had confessed.
athar_applications: Concrete, teen-understandable fact that confessions can be false; use with care and without real victims' details.
limitations: Advocacy organisation; DNA-exoneration cases are a non-random subset (mostly serious crimes in the US) and cannot give a general false-confession rate.

title: Psychological Strategies for Winning a Geopolitical Forecasting Tournament
key_findings: In a two-year geopolitical forecasting tournament, brief probability training (debiasing, reference classes, averaging estimates), teaming and tracking top performers each improved calibration and resolution.
Combining psychological interventions with statistical aggregation produced the most accurate forecasts.
athar_applications: Best available evidence that calibration is trainable with brief instruction plus feedback - supports ATHAR's calibration dashboard and 'think in base rates' micro-lessons.
limitations: Adult volunteer forecasters on geopolitical questions; teens and mystery-case contexts untested; abstract-level access.

title: Accuracy of forecasts in strategic intelligence
publisher: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
key_findings: Analysis of 1,514 real strategic-intelligence forecasts found good discrimination and calibration; miscalibration was mostly underconfidence.
Underconfidence was greater for harder and less policy-important forecasts; recalibration reduced it.
athar_applications: Nuance for ATHAR feedback: the calibration error can run both ways - the system should flag under- as well as over-confidence.
limitations: One national analytic unit; professional analysts; abstract-level access.

title: Reducing tunnel vision with a pen-and-paper tool for the weighting of criminal evidence
edition_version: Journal of Investigative Psychology and Offender Profiling 15(2):227-233
key_findings: Participants given an alternative (innocence) scenario alone did not reliably use it.
Adding a simple pen-and-paper task - rating how well each piece of evidence fits the primary hypothesis - helped reduce tunnel vision.
athar_applications: Key design evidence: merely showing an alternative suspect is not enough; ATHAR must make players actively rate evidence against hypotheses (light hypothesis board).
limitations: Short paper, vignette study, likely student sample; sample size and effect sizes not available in abstract; contrasts with mixed ACH results (ATH-SRC-0430).

title: Motivational sources of confirmation bias in criminal investigations: the need for cognitive closure
edition_version: Journal of Investigative Psychology and Offender Profiling 2(1):43-63
key_findings: Two experiments with 50 criminal investigators and 68 students reading a homicide case file; initial hypothesis framed by motive vs alternative perpetrator.

Investigators' need for cognitive closure moderated how they judged evidence strength and reacted to inconsistencies and alternative perpetrators; motivation, not only cognition, shapes confirmation bias.
athar_applications: Supports avoiding time-pressure mechanics that push premature closure; 'urge to close' is a motivational risk to design around.
limitations: Abstract reconstructed from index; direction of some subgroup effects ambiguous - check full text before citing specifics.

title: "He's guilty!": Investigator bias in judgments of truth and deception
key_findings: Signal-detection analysis: training and experience did not improve discrimination between truthful and deceptive statements.
Training/experience shifted response bias towards judging statements deceptive ('investigator bias').
athar_applications: Grounds the error 'the more I investigate, the more everyone looks like a liar'; ATHAR feedback should track a player's lie-judgement bias, not just accuracy.
limitations: North American sample; lab deception task; abstract-level access.

title: 'I saw the man who killed Anna Lindh!' An archival study of witnesses' offender descriptions
key_findings: Archival analysis of descriptions from 29 witnesses to a real 2003 homicide, checked against CCTV of the perpetrator: 42% of reported attributes were incorrect, including basic features like height and age.
Descriptions became more complete after the perpetrator's images were published in the media, but only for clothing; co-witness and post-event influence are possible explanations.
athar_applications: Rare real-world field evidence that complements lab findings; supports witness characters whose descriptions shift after 'news' appears in the case world.
limitations: Single high-profile case; small sample; archival data cannot isolate causes; abstract-level access. Do not depict the real case in ATHAR content.

title: Achieving Best Evidence in Criminal Proceedings: Guidance on interviewing victims and witnesses, and guidance on using special measures
edition_version: Fourth edition; first published 31 Jan 2022, last updated 21 Jun 2023
key_findings: Official England and Wales guidance on interviewing child and adult victims and witnesses, including video-recorded interviews for vulnerable and intimidated witnesses used as evidence-in-chief.
Describes itself as taking a victim-centred and trauma-informed approach.
athar_applications: Reference for portraying young/vulnerable witness scenes respectfully (KO-CD-05-004); OGL allows reuse with attribution.
limitations: Detailed content not read this session; UK-specific legal procedure.

title: Considering the opposite: A corrective strategy for social judgment
edition_version: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 47(6):1231-1243
key_findings: Two experiments (biased assimilation of evidence on social issues; biased hypothesis testing of personality impressions): inducing participants to 'consider the opposite', by instruction or by materials making opposite possibilities salient, corrected bias more than demand-laden instructions to be fair and unbiased.
athar_applications: Candidate grounding for the 'argue the other side / defend the suspect' mechanic; owned by Library 06 (cognitive science).
limitations: Abstract read via OpenAlex (2026-10-27 gap-fill); 1984 US student samples; effect sizes not extracted.

title: General Comment No. 32: Article 14: Right to equality before courts and tribunals and to a fair trial (CCPR/C/GC/32)
title_ar: التعليق العام رقم 32: المادة 14 - الحق في المساواة أمام المحاكم والهيئات القضائية وفي محاكمة عادلة
edition_version: CCPR/C/GC/32, 23 August 2007; official Arabic version available
key_findings: Para. 30: the presumption of innocence places the burden of proof on the prosecution, requires proof beyond reasonable doubt, gives the accused the benefit of doubt, and obliges public authorities not to prejudge guilt (e.g., public statements).

Para. 41: Art. 14(3)(g) means no direct or indirect physical or undue psychological pressure to obtain a confession; statements obtained in violation of Art. 7 must be excluded, with the burden on the State to show voluntariness.
Paras. 42-44: juveniles get at least adult guarantees plus special protection (parents/guardians, counsel, prompt hearing, a minimum age of criminal responsibility, diversion where appropriate).
Replaces General Comment No. 13.
athar_applications: Normative anchor for ATHAR's fairness guard: in-game characters and NPC officials must not publicly declare a suspect guilty before the case is resolved.
Any interview mechanic that rewards psychological pressure contradicts para. 41; such choices must be scored as errors and explained.
Juvenile-suspect storylines must reflect para. 42 safeguards (guardian, counsel).
limitations: Authoritative interpretation of the ICCPR, binding on States parties in interpretation only; not a private-actor rule. UN document reuse terms not stated on the page.

title: JDP 2-00: Intelligence, Counter-intelligence and Security Support to Joint Operations (4th Edition)
authors: UK Ministry of Defence, Development, Concepts and Doctrine Centre (DCDC)
key_findings: Evaluation judges two things separately: the reliability of the source (A completely reliable ... E unreliable, F cannot be judged) and the credibility of the information (1 confirmed by other sources ... 5 improbable, 6 cannot be judged); Table 3.1 calls this the NATO Intelligence Grading System, 'sometimes referred to as the Admiralty Code'.
The two ratings need not match (e.g., B5, E1); F6 does not mean worthless, only that there is not enough to judge.
Credibility is best assessed by corroboration, but contradictory information should not be discarded, and analysts must watch for circular reporting.
Gradings should be reviewed as more information arrives, partly to avoid confirmation bias; other grading approaches also exist.
athar_applications: Adopt the two-axis source/information grading as a clue-card mechanic for ages 16+ (with the simpler UK 3x5x2 system for 13-15).
Teach 'reliable source, improbable claim' and 'unreliable source, confirmed claim' as explicit cases; flag circular reporting as a planted trap.
limitations: Military intelligence doctrine, not evidentiary standards; grades are human judgments with no reliability data in the document.
Crown copyright with restrictive conditions of release: describe in our own words only; do not reproduce the table.

title: Manual on Investigative Interviewing for Criminal Investigation
authors: United Nations Department of Peace Operations
Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights
United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime
edition_version: Ref. DPO 2024.01; effective 1 Feb 2024; review date 1 Feb 2028
key_findings: The full manual (approved by the heads of DPO, OHCHR and UNODC) is the same publication as ATH-SRC-0404; this record captures its content, read in this round.

Treats false-evidence ploys, minimising or exaggerating consequences, and implied leniency as psychological abuse; confession-seeking interviewers are more prone to confirmation bias and contaminate memory.
Children and people with psychosocial or intellectual disabilities are especially vulnerable to suggestive questioning and pressure and more likely to confess falsely.
States that non-verbal behaviour and physiological responses are unreliable deception indicators and that lie-detection technologies are ineffective.
Structured around the six Méndez Principles and a step-by-step non-coercive interviewing process.
athar_applications: Validates ATHAR's ban on demeanour-as-evidence and on rewarded coercive dialogue options.
Use the manual's list of prohibited tactics as the authoritative 'red list' for interview-scene choices.
limitations: Normative guidance citing research; not itself an empirical study. Reuse terms of the UN PDF not stated.
